name: Facial nerve (CN VII)
summary: The facial nerve is really two nerves travelling together: the motor root to the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric, and the nervus intermedius carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal, nasal, submandibular and sublingual glands, and a little skin sensation from the ear. After looping over the abducens nucleus it leaves the pontomedullary junction, crosses the cerebellopontine angle with the eighth nerve into the internal acoustic meatus, and follows a long tortuous canal through the temporal bone (labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid segments) to the stylomastoid foramen and the parotid gland. Its lesion produces the peripheral facial palsy that involves the forehead, whereas a corticobulbar lesion spares it; the accompanying loss of taste, tearing or stapedius reflex tells you how far up the canal the lesion sits.

anatomy.location: Motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum → internal genu around the abducens nucleus → exit at the lateral pontomedullary junction (cerebellopontine angle) with the nervus intermedius and VIII → internal acoustic meatus (anterosuperior quadrant) → labyrinthine segment to the geniculate ganglion (greater petrosal nerve leaves) → tympanic segment along the medial wall of the middle ear (nerve to stapedius leaves) → mastoid segment (chorda tympani leaves) → stylomastoid foramen → through the parotid gland dividing into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

function: Facial expression and eye closure, stapedius reflex, taste from the anterior tongue and palate, lacrimation and salivation (except parotid), sensation of part of the external ear.

arteries: stylomastoid and petrosal branches of the external carotid

bestView.label: facial motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum and the genu over the abducens nucleus
nerve crossing the cerebellopontine angle into the internal acoustic meatus
geniculate ganglion and tympanic segment in the temporal bone

imaging.normalAppearance: The cisternal and canalicular segments are seen with the eighth nerve on thin T2 (CISS), the facial nerve anterosuperior in the meatus; the intratemporal course is mapped on temporal bone CT. Normal mild enhancement of the geniculate and tympanic segments exists; intense labyrinthine segment enhancement indicates Bell palsy or zoster, a mass indicates schwannoma or hemangioma. The HCP1065 mesh in this atlas shows the cisternal segment.

pathology.finding: Enhancement of the labyrinthine segment, geniculate ganglion and proximal tympanic segment without expansion.
Similar enhancement, often involving the eighth nerve and labyrinth, with vesicles in the ear.
Enhancing mass in the cerebellopontine angle and meatus compressing VII with VIII (and later V).

pathology.pathology: Pontine lesion at the facial nucleus or fascicle
pathology.finding: Caudal pontine infarct or plaque with peripheral-type facial palsy plus gaze palsy or contralateral hemiparesis.
Parotid mass with facial palsy: malignancy until proven otherwise (benign tumors do not paralyze the nerve).
Transverse fracture through the labyrinthine segment with immediate complete palsy.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MRI with contrast of the brainstem, cerebellopontine angle, temporal bone and parotid; temporal bone CT in trauma

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness of the whole hemiface including the forehead, incomplete eye closure, drooping mouth
lesionEffects.mechanism: Nucleus, nerve or branches (lower motor neuron)

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness of the lower face only with preserved forehead
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticobulbar (upper motor neuron) lesion: bilateral cortical input to the upper face

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of taste on the anterior tongue
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesion proximal to the chorda tympani (mastoid segment or above)
Lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius (tympanic segment or above)
Lesion at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion (greater petrosal nerve)

lesionEffects.deficit: Synkinesis, crocodile tears, hemifacial spasm after recovery
Emotional facial movement preserved with voluntary weakness (or the reverse)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dissociation between voluntary corticobulbar and emotional (limbic/thalamic) pathways

examination: Raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly (look for the Bell phenomenon and lash sign), show teeth, puff cheeks, whistle
Compare forehead with lower face: the key to central versus peripheral
Taste on the anterior tongue with sugar and salt
Ask about hyperacusis and dry eye; inspect the ear for vesicles
Examine VIII, V and VI for cerebellopontine angle and pontine lesions; palpate the parotid
pearls: Forehead spared: cortex or corticobulbar tract. Forehead involved: nucleus, nerve or muscle
Bell palsy is a diagnosis of exclusion: any palsy that is bilateral, recurrent, progressive over weeks, or accompanied by other cranial nerve signs needs imaging and serology (Lyme, HIV, sarcoid)

pitfalls: Eye protection is the urgent treatment of any peripheral facial palsy: lubricants and taping at night

nuclei.component: SVE: muscles of facial expression, stapedius
SVA: taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (rostral solitary nucleus)
GVE: superior salivatory nucleus (near the facial nucleus) for lacrimal, nasal, submandibular and sublingual glands

exit.brainstemExit: Lateral pontomedullary junction (cerebellopontine angle), motor root medial and nervus intermedius between it and VIII
exit.cisternalCourse: Cerebellopontine angle cistern with VIII and the AICA loop to the porus of the internal acoustic meatus
exit.foramen: Internal acoustic meatus (with VIII) → facial canal (fallopian canal) → stylomastoid foramen
exit.extracranialCourse: Through the parotid gland, dividing into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches to the muscles of facial expression and platysma

branches.name: Greater petrosal nerve
branches.supplies: parasympathetic to the lacrimal, nasal and palatine glands via the pterygopalatine ganglion; taste from the palate

branches.name: Chorda tympani
branches.supplies: taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; parasympathetic to the submandibular and sublingual glands via the lingual nerve

branches.name: Posterior auricular nerve
branches.supplies: occipitalis and auricular muscles; skin of the ear

branches.name: Nerves to stylohyoid and posterior digastric
Terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical)
branches.supplies: muscles of facial expression, buccinator, platysma

reflexes.name: Corneal (blink) reflex
reflexes.center: spinal trigeminal nucleus → both facial nuclei

reflexes.name: Glabellar tap
reflexes.efferent: orbicularis oculi (fails to habituate in Parkinson disease)

tests.name: Upper face
tests.how: Raise eyebrows, frown, close eyes tightly
tests.normal: Symmetric forehead wrinkling and eye closure
tests.abnormal: Weak forehead and incomplete closure in peripheral lesions; normal in central lesions

tests.name: Lower face
tests.how: Show teeth, puff cheeks, purse lips
tests.abnormal: Drooping angle, flattened nasolabial fold, cannot hold air

tests.name: Taste
tests.how: Sugar and salt on each side of the protruded anterior tongue
tests.abnormal: Loss on the affected side with lesions proximal to the chorda tympani

tests.name: Grading
tests.abnormal: Higher grades; complete palsy (VI) has a worse prognosis

lesionSigns.localisingValue: supranuclear (cortex, internal capsule, upper pons above the nucleus)

lesionSigns.sign: Forehead involved with ipsilateral gaze palsy or contralateral hemiparesis
Forehead involved with deafness, tinnitus or vertigo
lesionSigns.localisingValue: cerebellopontine angle or internal acoustic meatus

lesionSigns.sign: Forehead involved with dry eye, loss of taste and hyperacusis
Forehead involved with loss of taste but normal tearing
lesionSigns.localisingValue: tympanic or upper mastoid segment (below the geniculate, above the chorda)

lesionSigns.sign: Forehead involved with normal taste and tearing
lesionSigns.localisingValue: at or below the stylomastoid foramen (parotid, trauma)
Guillain–Barré, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, HIV, leptomeningeal disease

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear and fascicular lesions in the pons produce the same complete hemifacial weakness as nerve lesions but come with neighbors: an ipsilateral abducens palsy or gaze palsy (facial colliculus), contralateral hemiparesis (Millard–Gubler), and usually no taste or lacrimal change because those fibers join the nerve only at the cerebellopontine angle.
cranial.supranuclear: The upper facial subnucleus receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres and the lower subnucleus mainly from the contralateral hemisphere, so a stroke spares the forehead. Emotional smiling uses a separate limbic pathway, which explains the patient whose voluntary smile is weak but who smiles symmetrically at a joke (or vice versa).
